activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: The 800 metres draws on aerobic energy, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic energy, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly, so it feels like a sprint and a distance race at once.
story:
Katherine stood at the white line of lane four and watched Alex bounce on her toes the way she always did before the hundred metres, loose and jittery, like the start itself was the race. Miller leaned against the rail, arms crossed, patient as a fence post. "Eight hundred metres," Ms. Ferreira called from the infield. "Two laps. First one for both of you."

Alex tore through the opening curve so fast that Katherine's chest tightened just watching. Katherine held back, remembering her plan: even splits, steady legs, save something. By the end of the first lap Alex was ten metres ahead and Miller, the distance runner, was floating along beside Katherine as if the pace were nothing.

"She's gone," Miller said, nodding at Alex. "She always does that."

"She won't be gone at the two hundred mark," Katherine said. She had been working it out all week, lying on her bedroom floor with her race notes. Her legs felt like a sprinter's legs, quick and burning, but the race lasted almost two minutes, and two minutes was distance territory. Something invisible had to run out. She had read one word in the coach's old training manual, and Miller had given her the other half at lunch. "You said distance running is aerobic," she reminded him now. "Uses oxygen. And the other kind is anaerobic, works without oxygen but runs out fast." Miller nodded. That was the whole secret she had: the eight hundred wanted both at once, a sprint and a distance race together, and neither girl had ever tried it.

They passed the two hundred mark. Alex's shoulders had climbed up toward her ears, and her stride, so beautiful on the backstretch, had gone ragged. Katherine passed her at the final curve without sprinting, only holding her consistent rhythm, and crossed the line with her legs shaking but hers. Miller came in a second later, grinning. Alex folded over the infield grass, hands on her knees.

"I had you," Alex panted. "First whole lap."

"That was the problem," Katherine said, offering her a water bottle. She felt a flicker of envy at how easy the first lap had looked, so light and free, but it faded before it settled. "You spent everything on lap one. I saved a factor for the end. Storage. That's all it is."

Alex took a long drink, wiped her mouth and squinted at the line. "Okay. Same race tomorrow. I go out slower."

"You go out slower," Katherine agreed, and the two of them walked back toward the start.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Placing onion cells in salty water draws water out of them, so the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall and can be seen; this is called plasmolysis.
story:
The science museum's basement lab smelled faintly of vinegar and floor polish, and Alexander had been squinting into the same microscope for ten minutes. His worksheet had three blanks to fill in: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. He had found the wall easily, a neat row of brick-like boxes, and the nucleus showed up as a dark dot once Ms. Chen adjusted the light. The membrane stayed invisible. "It's like it doesn't want to be found," he muttered.

His lab partner Khalid leaned over from the next stool. "Mine's the same. I drew a dotted line and wrote maybe here." Alexander raised one eyebrow at him, and Khalid shrugged. "What? The line's sparse. It's an honest dotted line."

Ms. Chen drifted past their table, hands behind her back, and looked at Alexander's worksheet without touching it. "You have forty minutes before the bus commutes back to school," she said. "The bus commutes, not you. You just sit there." Then she moved on to argue gently with a boy who was trying to focus on his own eyelash.

Alexander sat back and thought. The membrane was there, everyone said so, but he couldn't see it. So the problem wasn't the membrane. The problem was that it was pressed against the wall, hiding along the edge, the way a curtain looks flat against a window. If something could pull the curtain inward, even a little, it would appear as its own line. He didn't know what could pull it. He turned the worksheet over and sketched a box with a smaller box inside it, then a smaller one inside that, like a target.

Khalid, meanwhile, had gotten bored and was experimenting with the little dropper bottles on the tray. One held clear water, one held salty water, and he added a drop of the salty one to his slide, just to see whether anything happened. He bent over the eyepiece and went very quiet. "Alexander. Come here. Now." Under the lens, the inner edge of each cell had shrunk away from the wall, pulled inward, and there it was: a second outline, a separate line, plain as anything. The dotted line on Khalid's worksheet was suddenly embarrassing to both of them.

"Salt water," Alexander said slowly, looking from the bottle to the slide. "Salt water did that." He wrote membrane in his first blank, then added in the margin: salt water makes it show. Khalid flipped to the glossary at the back of his handout and ran his finger down the page. "It's called plasmolysis," he announced, pleased with himself. "Plas-mo-ly-sis. Four syllables. That's worth extra credit at least."

Alexander carried his slide to the front to show Ms. Chen, holding it flat like a pizza. She looked at it, then at him, and tapped the margin note with one finger. "So," she said, "what would happen if you put a drop of plain water on next?" Alexander opened his mouth, then closed it. Khalid was already walking back toward the tray of dropper bottles. "Only one way to find out," he called over his shoulder.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
Jaxson typed the joke into the class group chat at his kitchen table: "Great, so our science project is due the same day as the field trip. Guess we'll present it from the bus."

Elyas replied within a minute, and it was not a joke back. "Wait, we have to present on the bus? Nobody told me that. Should I email Mr. Farah?" Then Jakob piled on: "I just texted my mom to drive my poster to school Friday."

Jaxson winced. He read his own message again. Without a face or a voice, "Guess we'll present it from the bus" sounded like a real plan. He typed "It was a joke" and watched three dots appear, disappear, and appear again while Elyas decided whether to be annoyed.

He went looking for how people fixed this problem, because it had to be an old problem. On a page about the history of online messages, he found a post from a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman. On September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, he had proposed the emoticon :-) so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Jaxson read it twice. A sideways smiley face, invented for exactly this, forty-some years before Elyas panicked about a bus.

He copied the smiley into his next message. "We'll present in class like normal. Friday is just the trip :-)"

"Ha. Okay," Elyas wrote. "You scared me." Jakob sent back a single thumbs-up. Jaxson tried it again on his mother, who was washing dishes and checking her phone at the same time. He texted "The dishwasher ate my homework" from across the room. She turned around, frowning, phone in hand. Then her screen refreshed with the second message, " :-) ", and she went back to the dishes, indifferent to the whole exchange now that the joke was marked.

There was one anomaly left in the chat. Elyas had sent "Mr. Farah says we DO have to bring the project on the bus for the ride home" with no smiley anywhere. Jaxson stared at it. Was that a joke, revenge for the earlier scare, or the actual truth? He typed "really?" and added a colon and a parenthesis, then deleted it, because on this one he needed the words to carry nothing but their plain meaning. He picked up his phone and called.

"It's real," Elyas said. "I asked him after last period."

Jaxson looked at the group chat, where Jakob had just posted a row of laughing faces under the exact news that had made Jaxson panic twice in one evening. He typed back, "So the one true thing in this chat is the thing I almost didn't believe. :-)"

"Delete the smiley," Jakob wrote. "I'm saving a screenshot for Mr. Farah."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
The phone reached Logan's cousin first, passed hand to hand over the plates of Aunt Rosa's seven-layer dip like a secret too heavy to hold. "It's blue and black," his cousin said. "Obviously." Logan leaned across the table to look, and what he saw was a lumpy, badly lit dress that was clearly, undeniably white and gold.

"No way." He grabbed the phone and turned the screen toward his mother. "Mom. Tell me what color this is."

"White and gold," she said, without even squinting. "Why, what's wrong with you?"

The kitchen split in half within a minute. Uncle Pete bellowed "blue and black" from the grill, and Aunt Rosa agreed, and Logan's grandmother, still holding the potato salad, said it was white with gold lace, and suddenly nobody was eating. The photo had started circulating online that afternoon, his cousin explained, and it seemed like the whole internet was arguing about it too. Logan's phone buzzed twice in his pocket: Aryanna texting IT'S WHITE AND GOLD, NO DEBATE, and Briana texting back LOL it's blue and black, check your eyes.

Here was Logan's problem, and it was a real one. He had told Aryanna and Briana he would settle it before the family's annual talent show started at eight, because the three of them had agreed to report a winner to their group chat, and Logan had impulsively promised an answer by then. It was 7:41. The living room clock ticked like it was counting down something worse than a dress.

He could not understand it. Same screen, same photo, same kitchen light, and yet his mother saw white and gold while Uncle Pete, standing two feet away, saw blue and black. That meant the difference had to be in the people, not the picture, and if it was in the people, maybe it was something about their eyes, or something he couldn't see directly at all. He had a simple idea. He would pass the phone slowly around the table, one person at a time, and write down what each person saw in order, like a scientist collecting samples. Maybe a pattern would show.

"Grandma," he said, sliding the phone toward her. "Just the color. Nothing else." She said white and gold. Uncle Pete, blue and black. Aunt Rosa, blue and black. His mother, white and gold, again, with feeling. His cousin took the phone, stared, frowned, and said, slowly, "Wait. Now it looks white and gold. It looked blue before." The whole kitchen went quiet. Logan wrote that down twice and underlined it, his stamina for polite small talk now entirely spent; he had a deadline.

At 7:58 he typed his report: family split in half, cousin switched sides mid-stare, no winner. Then his cousin's phone buzzed with news that the actual company that made the dress had confirmed the real dress was blue and black. Logan read it aloud, and Uncle Pete slammed the table like his team had won the championship, and his mother said, "Then what am I looking at?"

"Tomorrow, same picture," Aryanna texted, just as Briana sent, "Send it again, I want to prove myself right."

Logan held up his phone and took the vote one last time, and his grandmother, arms crossed, said, "White. Gold. Forever."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
story:
The messages about Constance started appearing in the group chat on Tuesday, and by Wednesday they were gone. Stella had seen them, though. Someone with the username DragonByte88 had written that Constance smelled like the bus and that nobody should sit with her at lunch. When Stella scrolled back to show her mom, the messages had been deleted, and the chat looked innocent, all smiley faces and homework questions.

She thought about it all through math. The deleted messages were like footprints in sand at the beach near her grandmother's house; the tide took them, and later nobody could prove anyone had walked there at all. But her phone had a camera button, didn't it? If mean comments could vanish before a kid showed anyone, then a screenshot would keep them. She tested the idea right there under her desk, taking a picture of a silly message Leonidas had sent about the cafeteria meatloaf. The screenshot went into her photos and stayed.

"Constance is going to quit the robotics team," Leonidas said at lunch, poking at his tray. "She told me her mom makes a long commute to work, and she doesn't want to bother her with kid stuff."

"Kid stuff," Stella repeated. She watched Constance sit alone at the end of the table, arranging her sandwich like it was an intricate machine, each piece placed exactly. "It's not kid stuff if it makes you quit something you love."

That night, Stella almost sent a message to DragonByte88 herself, something sharp and satisfying. She typed it out and stared at it. But calling someone names would just make a new adversary, and the whole point was to make things better, not louder. She deleted her draft, which felt strange, using the same power that had been used against Constance. Then she took three more screenshots the next time the mean messages appeared, capturing the username and the time, and walked them to Mr. Eze's classroom before first period.

Mr. Eze looked at the photos for a long moment. "This is a record," he said quietly. "Thank you."

By Friday, DragonByte88 had been identified, and there was a meeting with parents that nobody would describe in detail. Constance came back to robotics, and she stood beside Stella at the workbench, soldering a circuit board with steady hands. But something had shifted anyway. Leonidas had been DragonByte88, and though he said sorry twice, his voice cracking, Constance only nodded at him now instead of laughing with him. Stella had done the right thing, and it had cost her a friend's easy trust. She picked up her own soldering iron and watched Constance guide the tip along the wire.

"Hold it steady," Constance said. "Like that."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Sarah had meant to finish her lab report, but the cursor blinked at the top of an empty page while she kept thinking about lunch. Cashton had walked into the cafeteria holding a smoothie from the juice place at the mall, and Edward had said, "I knew you were at the mall. You were in the game store at four." Cashton had not told anyone where he was going.

She turned to the computer next to hers, where Edward was pretending to research volcanoes. "How did you know which store?" she asked. "Did Cashton text you?"

"Nope." Edward grinned and pulled his phone under the desk. "Look. It's called Snap Map." On his screen, a map of the town, and on the map a small face with Cashton's photo on it, sitting right on top of the game store at the mall. Another dot sat at the soccer field, where some of their classmates had practice. "It shows real-time location, like right now," Edward said. "He's my friend on Snapchat, so I can see him whenever."

Sarah looked at the map for a long moment. She had Snapchat too. That meant people on her friends list could see her dot wherever she went, every day, without her saying a word. It was a strange feeling, like learning that the walls of the computer lab were glass and everyone walking past could watch her type. Nobody had conveyed this to her directly; she had simply never looked.

Mr. Nakamura came by and leaned over her shoulder. "Report on rocks, not phones, Sarah." She nodded and typed a sentence about sedimentary layers, but her mind was still on the map. She had a way to test it. At the end of class she found Cashton at his locker and asked him to walk to the library after school, then told Edward nothing. If Edward could name the library before evening, the map was showing her too, not just Cashton.

At three thirty she and Cashton sat in the library with a geography book between them, mostly as camouflage, since neither of them needed it. At 3:40 her phone buzzed. A message from Edward: "Why are you two at the library? Boring."

She held the screen so Cashton could see it. "You didn't tell him anything?"

"Nothing," Cashton said. He pulled out his own phone and started tapping through screens, frowning. "There's some setting in here. Ghost Mode, it says."

"Turn it on," Sarah said. She watched his dot vanish from her own map, an empty street where a face had been a second before. "Now do mine."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
Theodore carried his chili and his chocolate milk through the cafeteria like a full tray of treasure, because today was the day of the sixth-grade talent show sign-up, and Bryson had promised to save them a spot as a comedy duo. The cafeteria smelled like disinfectant and french fries, and a line of ants had begun to colonize the corner by the vending machines, which everyone agreed was going to become a whole crisis by Friday. Then someone's shoulder slammed into his tray, and the chili went airborne, and the tray clattered onto the floor with a noise that turned every head in the room.

Bryson was standing right there, laughing.

"Nice one," Theodore said, picking up his milk before it rolled away. His ears felt hot. "Real funny."

"I didn't do that on purpose," Bryson said, still grinning, which made it worse.

"You were literally standing there waiting for me." Theodore dumped the tray on the counter with a bang. "Forget the talent show. Do it with somebody else."

He walked to the far table where Julie was sketching in her notebook. She pushed her own fries toward him without looking up, which was the kindest thing anyone had done all lunch period.

" Bryson shoved my tray on purpose," Theodore said. He told her the whole thing: the waiting, the laughing, the chili everywhere. Julie tapped her pencil on the page. On the cover of her notebook was a psychology article she'd printed out, something she'd been quoting all week, mostly to win arguments.

"You know what you might have," she said. "Hostile attribution bias."

"What is that, a disease?"

"It's when you assume somebody meant to hurt you, but what they did was unclear and could totally have been an accident." She shrugged. "My article says everybody does it."

Theodore looked across the cafeteria. Bryson was mopping near the soda machine with a wad of napkins, and a janitor was setting up a yellow caution cone. A caution cone. Theodore stood up so fast his chair squeaked.

He crossed the room, and there it was: a greasy, gray smear on the tiles right where he'd been walking, half cleaned, slick as ice. Bryson pointed at it with a shaking napkin.

"I slipped," Bryson said. "I grabbed for anything, and that was your tray. I was laughing because I almost ate the floor. I was saving you a seat, you doughnut, for the talent show."

Theodore crouched down and touched the edge of the smear with one finger. It slid like a skating rink. He looked up at the ceiling and let out a laugh that surprised even him.

"So it wasn't you. It was the floor." He held up his slick finger as evidence, like a lawyer in the shows his dad watched. "The floor ambushed us both."

"Is the duo still on?" Bryson asked. "Because I already told Mr. Li we're doing the bit about the cafeteria food."

"You told Mr. Li already?" Mr. Li, who ran the talent show and also taught social studies, was currently explaining to a table of eighth graders why the new rule about hats had become so controversial, and why the school budget looked like a small recession had hit the drama department alone. He waved when he spotted them.

"Sign-up sheet's on my door after lunch," he called over.

Theodore grabbed a roll from Bryson's untouched tray and pointed it at him like a microphone. "The duo is on. But you're playing the guy who slips in the grease."

"Deal," said Bryson, "but I get to wear the caution cone."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: In a canyon wall, harder rock layers tend to form steep cliffs and softer layers wear back into gentler slopes, which gives the Grand Canyon its stepped walls.
story:
The exhibit hall had a model river built into a long steel table, and water circulated through it from a pump underneath, dragging a slow load of sand from one end to the other. Hudson stood in front of it with his notebook open and nothing written. Tomorrow he had to explain to Mr. Njoroge's class how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and so far all he had was a title with two words underlined: erosion and deposition.

"You've been staring at that water for ten minutes," Alexi said, hopping up beside him. Alexi had stayed home sick on Tuesday with some virus and was still carrying tissues everywhere, so Hudson shifted his bag to make room on the rail.

"I'm missing something," Hudson said. Behind them a wall-sized screen showed the Grand Canyon in colors so extravagant, all orange and rose and purple shadow, that other kids kept taking pictures of it instead of the model. Hudson had done the same thing at first. Then he had noticed the canyon walls.

He pointed at the screen. "Look at the sides. They're not smooth. They go down in steps. Flat ledge, then a steep drop, then another ledge." He flipped his notebook to the sketch he'd made of the photograph, tracing the shape with his pencil: staircases, everywhere, on both walls.

"So?" Alexi said.

"So the river cuts down, that part I get. But why the steps?" Hudson turned back to the model. The museum had built the banks out of stacked layers, and he could see the same thing happening there in miniature, if he was reading it right. One dark, chunky layer stuck out over the softer sandy layers beneath it, which had worn back into gentle slopes. He grabbed the spare hose the museum kept for visitors and let a trickle of extra water run down the edge of the bank, then watched. The soft layers slumped away grain by grain. The hard layer above held, jutting out farther and farther, until a chunk finally broke off and tumbled down.

"That's it," Hudson said, scribbling fast. "Hard layers make the steep cliffs, soft layers wear back into slopes. The river does the rest over millions of years. That's where the steps come from." He showed Alexi the page, arrow by arrow.

Alexi blew his nose and studied it. "Draw the ledge bigger," he said. "Mr. Njoroge likes big ledges."

Hudson grinned and darkened the overhanging layer until it looked ready to fall.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The independent variable is the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens.
story:
Zoey knelt in the garden behind the science wing, where four tomato plants stood in a row under the afternoon sun. Three of them stood tall and green, but the fourth drooped, its leaves curled like old paper. Something was hurting it, and whatever that something was, she could not see it. "Maybe it's the water," Roxane said, crouching beside her. "Or the soil. Or bugs we can't find." Zoey pulled a notebook from her back pocket and wrote all three guesses down. A guess you could test, her brother had once told her, was worth more than a guess you could only argue about, and she intended to test every one.

She remembered last summer, when she and her cousin had built paper airplanes in the garage. They had wanted a plane that could cross the whole driveway, so they switched to heavier paper and folded a new wing shape at the same time. The plane flew beautifully, but when they high-fived each other, her cousin shrugged and admitted something that bugged Zoey for days. "We can't tell which one did it," he had said. "We changed two things." The plane went in the scrap bin, and they started over with the old wing shape on the new paper, just to see.

That memory was why she held up a hand now when Roxane reached for the watering can and a bag of fertilizer at the same time. "Stop. If we change both, we won't know which one mattered." Roxane frowned at her. "So we only change one thing?" "Right. The independent variable is the one thing you change on purpose," Zoey said, "and we only get one." They picked water first. The drooping plant got its usual feeding and no extra water for two days, while the healthy plants carried on as always. Nothing improved, so they crossed water off the list.

The next test was soil. Zoey dug gently at the base of the sick plant and found the ground packed hard and damp while the other beds crumbled loose and dry. She and Roxane loosened the soil around the roots and mixed in sand from the pile by the shed, changing nothing else. The watering can stayed on the bench. The fertilizer bag stayed rolled shut.

On the third morning, Daphne came out to see, and the three of them formed a small jury of observers, crouching in a half circle around the plant. The lowest leaves had lifted off the ground, and the stem stood straighter where it had bent before. "It's working," Daphne whispered, as though loudness might undo it. Zoey wrote the date in her notebook, then drew a small arrow pointing at the plant, and underlined one word twice. Behind them, Ms. Adeyemi unlatched the gate with a bundle of stakes in her arm, and Roxane called over her shoulder, "We only changed one thing, Ms. Adeyemi. Come look at the leaves."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
The marigolds rode in William's lap all the way home, wrapped in wet paper towel, so lush and orange they seemed to glow against the gray seat. His mother drove slowly, the way she had all week, and the photo of Grandma Elena sat faceup on the dashboard between them. Nobody had said much since the funeral, and William was tired of the quiet, so he turned the problem over in his mind instead.

Kristina had explained it to him on Friday, leaning against the lockers while he pretended he didn't care. "November first and second," she'd said. "Dia de los Muertos. My mom builds an altar every year, with pictures and marigolds. They're called ofrendas." She had shrugged like it was nothing, but then she'd pressed a paper bag of marigold petals into his hand, ones left over from her family's table, and said, "The color and the scent are supposed to guide spirits home."

Home. That was the part William kept circling back to. His mother would set up the ofrenda in the living room tomorrow, November first, with the photo and the flowers, exactly the way it was supposed to be done. But William could not stop thinking that Grandma Elena had spent half her life in this car. She had driven him to school and to practice and to the lake every summer, singing off key with the windows cracked. If scent guided a spirit home, then didn't the car count as home too? He couldn't see a spirit, couldn't test for one directly, but he could test the idea anyway, the way he tested anything: set it up and watch what happened.

"You assume I'm going to say no," his mother said, catching his eye in the mirror as they pulled into the driveway.

"I haven't even asked yet."

"You've been staring at that photo for six blocks. Ask."

"Can we leave the flowers in here tonight? Just some of them. Next to her picture." He picked up a few petals and let them fall toward the dashboard, one by one, so they landed in a loose trail around the frame. "It's not a whole ofrenda. It's more like a... mechanism. Like a signal."

His mother looked at the petals, then at the photo, and something in her shoulders came down an inch. "She did love this ugly car," she said. She unbuckled but didn't open her door. Instead she reached over, straightened the frame so Grandma Elena faced the windshield, toward the road she'd driven a thousand times.

"Leave the window cracked," William said. "So the scent gets out."

His mother turned the key back one click and lowered the window, and the cold air moved through the marigolds and out into the dark. "Goodnight, Mom," she said, and William scattered the last petal onto the dash, bright orange against the fading light.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
story:
The washing machines lived in a back corner of the school's life skills room, and Ms. Navarro had posted a sign above them that read, in cheerful letters, DO YOUR OWN LAUNDRY SO NOBODY HAS TO DO IT FOR YOU. Rosalie's first assignment was a towel, which was forgiving. Her second assignment was Titus's gym shirt, which was not. There was a pizza-grease stain on the front, roughly the shape of Italy, and water alone had done nothing to it. She knew this because of Friday.

On Friday, she had dropped a slice of pizza on her own shirt at lunch, and Avah had told her to just rinse it in the fountain, which she did, and the stain had stayed exactly where it was, only wetter. "Water hates that stain," Avah had observed, and Rosalie had carried the shirt around all afternoon like an ambiguous trophy, since she couldn't decide whether it counted as a disaster or as evidence.

On Monday she cornered Titus at the sorting table, where he was confidently putting a red sock in with the whites. "Your shirt," she said. "It has grease on it." Titus looked at the stain the way you look at a bug you are not planning to touch. "My grandma washes it and it comes out," he said. "She uses the blue bottle. I don't know what's in it. She calls it detergent."

Rosalie wrote that in her notebook, because Ms. Navarro had told them to document each load from sorting to folding. Then she ran a test. She cut two patches from an old pillowcase Ms. Navarro kept for disasters, rubbed a little margarine from the cooking station into both, and washed one in plain water and one with detergent. The plain water patch came out greasy. The detergent patch came out clean. She held them up beside each other for a long moment, feeling like she'd caught something in the act.

That afternoon she found a note in her locker, folded into a triangle, which was Avah's signature move. It read: "Did the fountain thing work? Asking for my brother. His whole hoodie is one stain." Rosalie wrote back on the same triangle: "No. Come to the washing machines after last bell. Bring the hoodie."

When Avah arrived, hoodie in hand, Rosalie didn't lecture her. She just showed her the two patches, then poured detergent into the machine while Avah watched the hoodie tumble. "So the soap grabs the grease?" Avah said slowly. Rosalie nodded. "Detergent molecules have one end that's attracted to water and another end that's attracted to oil and grease," she said. "So they lift the grease off into the wash water." Avah frowned. "That's a weird metaphor for soap." "It's not a metaphor," Rosalie said. "It's just what soap does." Avah considered this, then leaned against the machine until it was time to pull the hoodie out, warm and clean and folded badly, and neither of them said anything at all.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: India's summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because its moist winds blow in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea.
story:
Alexandre had promised Ms. Teo a five-minute talk on the monsoon, and the talk was tomorrow morning, and he was stuck at his grandfather's house with no internet and one crumpled page of notes. The notes said one thing he trusted: India's summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because its moist winds blow in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea. He had copied it down in class without really looking at it, which he was starting to regret, the way he regretted not asking questions back in September when the unit began.

"It's due when?" his grandfather asked, setting a cup of tea on the table with a copper spoon in it.

"Tomorrow. First period."

"Then we'd better figure out what you actually want to say." His grandfather had farmed a small plot as a boy, and he never let Alexandre forget it, although he never lectured either. He just waited, which was worse.

Alexandre spread the notes flat and frowned at them. "The part I keep losing is the arrow on the weather map. It points from the sea toward the land, from the bottom left. Fatima drew it for me and said her uncle checks these maps before every fishing trip, so it's real. But I can't picture why the wind matters so much until I say it out loud."

His grandfather tapped the spoon. "You can't see wind, but you can see what it carries. When I was young, we would dry chili peppers on the roof, and if the wind came off the wet fields instead of off the dry hill, they took twice as long. My mother could read the roof like a page." He sipped his tea. "That spoon, by the way. Copper is a fine conductor of heat. Useful for stirring, useless for staying cool in your hand."

Alexandre looked at the spoon, then at the kettle steaming on the stove, and an idea arrived all at once. He went and got the small desk fan from the bedroom, a bowl of water, and a dry dish towel. He wet one end of the towel, draped it over the bowl, and set the fan so it blew across the wet cloth toward the towel's dry end. Within a minute the dry end felt damp. He turned the fan, aimed it away, and the dampness stopped spreading.

"It's the sea," he said. "The wind comes in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea, and it's carrying water the whole way, like the fan carrying it off the wet cloth. It's called the southwest monsoon because of where the wind comes from, not where the rain lands. That's the thing I had backwards." He paused, half pleased and half embarrassed. "It's ironic, honestly. I spent an hour memorizing the words and never once asked which way the wind was blowing."

"And why does it matter, for the farmers?" his grandfather asked, because of course he would.

"Because rice needs that water. The fields drink what the wind brings. If the winds are weak that year, there isn't enough, and if they're late, the planting is late, and people like Fatima's uncle watch the maps like my grandmother watched your roof." He picked up his pencil. "I'm going to open with the fan. I'll ask Willa to hold the wet cloth."

His grandfather smiled into his cup and said, "Bring the copper spoon too."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
Camille slid the old poster across the history classroom table so Eugene and Arabella could see it. A smiling soldier held up a cup of coffee, and above him, in letters as tall as his helmet, the words EVERYONE'S DOING IT. Underneath, a movie star Camille didn't recognize gave a thumbs up beside the slogan.

"Who is that?" Eugene asked.

"A famous actress back then," Camille said. "That's the whole trick. They put her face on it so people think, if she drinks this coffee, I should too." She tapped the EVERYONE'S DOING IT. "And this part makes it sound like the whole country already agreed. Nobody wants to be the one person left out."

Arabella frowned at the poster. "So they never actually say the coffee is good."

"Not once," Camille said. "Not one word about the coffee."

Mr. González had assigned them a poster project for Friday, and Camille wanted theirs to be the one he hung on the wall. But when she'd searched the library database for wartime posters, she'd found something better than posters. A dusty book about a group that called itself the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, founded in the United States in 1937, when the whole country was arguing about whether to join the war. The book said the Institute tried to teach ordinary people how to recognize propaganda. Camille had read that sentence three times. Regular people, in 1937, learning to spot the same tricks she was pointing at on this poster.

"Okay," Eugene said, "so we put the poster on our board and write, this is a trick."

"That's just accusing the poster of lying," Camille said. "It doesn't show anything. We need to prove it's a trick." She'd been testing an idea on the bus, and it had worked. She pulled out a page from a magazine. It showed a basketball player grinning next to a bottle of sports drink. Below him, the words MILLIONS OF FANS ALREADY KNOW.

"Same tricks," she said. "Eighty years apart. Celebrity face, everybody's-doing-it. If we put the old poster and this ad side by side, people can see the pattern for themselves. We don't have to say a word."

Arabella leaned closer to the magazine page. "It's like a rodent in the kitchen," she said. "You never see it. You just find the same bite marks on two different loaves of bread, and then you know."

"That's grim," Eugene said, "but yes."

Mr. González wandered over and looked at their two posters for a long moment. "The Institute would have liked this," he said quietly, and walked on before Camille could ask which institute.

She wrote it on the board anyway, in small letters at the bottom: Spot the pattern. Then she stood back next to her poster and waited to see who would stop and look.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
Justin pushed through the glass door of Remedy Pharmacy with his grandmother's list in his fist: ginger tea, the kind advertised on the radio. Three days ago she had suffered the worst headache of her life, and yesterday, after one cup of the tea, she swore it was gone. She had sent him a text that morning: "That tea is a miracle. Buy me six boxes." He was willing to buy the tea, but something about it bothered him, the way a loose tooth bothers your tongue.

At the counter he ran into Colton, who was picking up an inhaler for his little brother. Colton held up his phone. "Look at this review site. Five hundred people say the tea fixed their headaches. Five hundred people can't be wrong, right?" Justin scrolled through the reviews and noticed something. Every single one started the same way: "I had the worst headache ever, and then..." Not one person had written in about a mild headache. He said it out loud, slowly. "Nobody with an ordinary headache bothered to write." The cashier rang up six boxes while the boys stood there, and Justin paid with his grandmother's ten dollars.

On the walk home, he stopped past Ms. Wang's classroom window, where she was stacking papers. He had a question from science class anyway, about why a vaccine gets tested against a fake shot instead of just being given to sick people. She answered that part quickly, and then he mentioned the tea. He said, "The worst headaches are the ones people try things on." She smiled and said only, "It's called regression to the mean," and went back to her papers. Justin repeated the phrase to himself all the way down the block.

He decided to test it, because Grandma drank the tea only when her head hurt badly, so her improvement might just coincide with the tea instead of being caused by it. That evening he made a chart on graph paper: date, headache level from one to ten, whether she drank the tea. Colton contributed his own column, headaches his mom reported, since Colton wanted to see the pattern too and prove or disprove it with more than one person. For eleven days the boxes went back and forth between them, filled with numbers.

The results stacked up. Grandma's terrible eights and nines were always followed by fives and fours, tea or no tea. Her mild threes stayed mild, or sometimes vanished on their own. One Saturday she had a nine, skipped the tea because they were out, and felt fine by Sunday anyway. Justin texted Colton a photo of the finished chart with the caption "The tea does nothing. The pattern does." Colton texted back a single word: "Fundamental." Grandma still drank her tea every night, because she liked it, and Justin didn't argue. He just taped the chart inside his science notebook, right next to the vaccine question.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and old carpet, and in the middle of it sat the world's most eccentric drum kit, a hulking thing Abdullah's dad had painted silver with a lightning bolt down the bass drum. Easton plugged in his keyboard and flipped open the sheet music to "Storm Warning," the piece their band was supposed to play at the school talent show on Friday. The problem was simple and enormous: every time they reached the last eight bars, half the band slowed down and the other half charged ahead, so the ending sounded like a car crashing into a parade.

"Again," Easton said. "From bar forty."

Leanne sighed and retuned her bass, which she had now done four times, purely out of despair. Abdullah counted them in, and for a while it actually held together. Then they hit the word printed above the final bars, the little italic word that had been ruining their week, and it happened again. Abdullah's cymbals swelled and slowed like a wave settling, while Leanne charged through the last chord at full speed and landed three beats early. The crash rang in the empty garage.

"Okay," Easton said, holding up both hands like a diplomat negotiating a hostage release. "Nobody move. Leanne, when you see that word, what do you do?"

"Nothing! I keep time, because that's my entire job in this band."

Easton looked at the page. "But why would the composer print a word if it means do nothing?" He tapped the word with his pencil, thinking. Abdullah slowed at it. Abdullah, who had never had a lesson and played entirely by ear, slowed. Leanne, who read every note like a rule carved in stone, did not. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something. "Abdullah, play the ending alone. Just you."

Abdullah played it, and sure enough his drums rolled slower and slower, the way thunder fades after a storm. Easton felt something click. "It's telling us to slow down. Gradually. That's the whole point of it."

Leanne leaned over the page and groaned. "It means gradually slowing down. Ritardando. I've been treating it like decoration this entire time." She narrowed her eyes at the opposite marking a few bars earlier. "And this one, accel-something, means gradually speeding up, which is why you two always raced ahead there while I kept plodding."

"I despise Italian," Abdullah announced cheerfully, twirling a drumstick. "It hides secrets."

They ran it once more, and this time when the word came, Leanne eased off with them, the whole band breathing together into one long, slowed final chord. Abdullah hit the crash cymbal and let it shimmer into silence.

"Now that," Easton said, "sounded like weather."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
story:
Vincent typed his program into the computer in the school lab, checked it twice, and hit run. The prompt appeared in black text on the white screen: enter a number. He typed 97, and the program printed prime. He tried 91 and got not prime, which was correct, since 91 was secretly 7 times 13. His program worked. The problem was what to do with it.

"I'm going to find the biggest prime," he told Kaylie, who sat two computers over. "I'll run a census of numbers, starting at two, and keep going until the program finds the last prime. Then I'll be famous."

Kaylie leaned over. "You know you can't, right?"

"Watch me. I'll test a hundred numbers at a time."

She pulled a math book out of her bag, the one Ms. Nwosu kept on the shelf for early finishers, and flipped until she found the page. "Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers." She slid the book across so he could see the page himself.

Vincent read the sentence twice. "Infinitely many. So there's no biggest one."

"There's no last one. It says proved, so it's not a guess."

He sat back and looked at his program. The prompt still blinked on the screen, waiting. If the primes never stopped, his plan to compress all of them into one final answer was dead. But a different idea came to him, and he tested it right there. He changed the program so that instead of asking for one number, it counted upward on its own and printed every prime it found. Then he added a line so it would never stop.

"Try 13,055," said Linkin from the next row, wandering over. "My cousin says it's exceptional, whatever that means."

The counter was in the nine thousands. They watched the primes scroll past, 9341, 9343, 9371, while Linkin pulled up a chair. When the counter reached 13055, the program printed not prime.

"Your cousin lied," Vincent said.

"Or the number lied." Linkin pointed at the screen. "It's still going, though. How long will it run?"

"Until the bell," Vincent said. "Euclid says it won't run out."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
Piper slid the paper across the counter at the eyeglass store and read it again while the clerk typed into the computer. It said -2.00 under the word sphere, and next to that, OD and OS, which she guessed meant right eye and left eye. She turned to Maia, who was leaning on the counter beside her.

"I got a minus two," Piper said. "On my eyes. That can't be good. What happens if you get all the way to zero?"

Maia peered at the paper. "It's not a score. My cousin has glasses. It's how they measure lens strength, in diopters. The minus sign means nearsighted, and a plus sign means farsighted." She tapped the counter. "So minus two just means your lenses are a certain strength, that's all."

Piper wanted to test that. If minus meant nearsighted, then nearsighted people should see far away badly but close up fine. She walked to the end of the store, where a rack of sunglasses stood by the entrance, and looked back at the eye chart hanging behind the counter. The big E at the top was clear, but the second line was a gray smear. Then she pulled her library book from her backpack and read the tiny copyright page from eight inches away, easy. Far blurry, near fine. Minus fit. She walked back.

"There you are," Maia said. "I've been doing a census. Nine people came in while you were gone, and six of them were picking up glasses. That's a lot for one store."

"You counted them?"

"I want to prove to Francisco that half the kids in our grade wear glasses. He says it's only a few. He's at the book display by the fountain if you want to argue with him."

While the clerk fitted the new frames to Piper's face and bent the arms behind her ears, Maia texted Francisco. The frames were thin and blue, and when Piper looked up, the store sharpened all at once, like someone had cleaned a window. She could read the sale sign across the aisle. She could read the small print on the lens cleaner box.

They found Francisco by the fountain, next to a traveling exhibit from the science museum, a glass case of live orchids with a card about the bees that pollinate them, and a model of a venomous snake with a warning never to touch a real one. Piper stopped in front of the exhibit sign at what had to be forty feet.

"That sign says the bees visit each flower twice a day," she said. "It's printed in letters this big." She held up her thumb and forefinger, a tiny gap between them.

Francisco squinted at the sign. "There's a sign?"
"How many kids in our grade wear glasses?" Maia asked him.
Francisco looked from the sign to Piper's new blue frames. "Okay. Maybe more than a few."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
The mosque hall smelled of cardamom and fried bananas, and Paige stood near the door holding a tin of her mother's lemon squares like it was a bomb about to go off. Dastan had invited her to the open house after Friday prayers, and she had said yes before thinking it through. Now she was surrounded by people who all seemed to know exactly what to do, and she did not know anything. The evening felt sophisticated in a way she couldn't name, full of small signals she couldn't read yet. She wished she were back home helping her dad with the leaky plumbing under the kitchen sink, where at least a problem was a problem and not a mystery.

Dastan appeared beside her with his little cousin hanging off his elbow. "You came! Come meet my grandmother." Paige followed him across the hall, rehearsing what to say. When they reached a small woman in a green headscarf, Paige remembered the tin and held it out. The grandmother smiled, but Dastan's aunt, standing nearby, caught Paige's wrist gently and murmured, "The other hand." Paige stared down. She had offered the gift with her left hand. Nobody had said a word about hands, and yet somehow she had already gotten it wrong.

At the long table afterward, Paige decided to verify her suspicion. She watched each person in turn, the way her dad watched a pipe joint before declaring it fixed. Every single one of them took the rice with the right hand, passed the mango drink with the right hand, waved away extra chicken with the right hand. Even Dastan's cousin, who was maybe five, did it. It wasn't random. It was a pattern, a rule she could actually learn, and learning a rule was something Paige knew how to do. When the satay platter came around, she reached for it with her right hand, and Dastan's grandmother gave her a nod so small that Paige almost missed it.

"So the right hand for everything," Paige said quietly to Dastan as they cleared plates. "Eating, giving, taking." He shrugged. "In Indonesia and Malaysia, it's a sign of respect. My whole family does it." She filed that away, feeling the evening loosen around her. She was about to carry a stack of cups to the kitchen when Dean came skidding in late from soccer practice, still in his muddy shorts, holding a box of dates as a gift.

Dean spotted Dastan's grandmother, walked straight up to her, and thrust the box out with his right hand, because Paige had already texted him the rule twice. The grandmother looked at the box, then lifted her arm, and Paige saw for the first time the plaster cast running from wrist to knuckle. "Thank you," the grandmother said, taking the dates carefully in her left hand. Behind her, Dastan whispered, "She broke it bowling." Dean looked at his own clean right hand, then at her full one, and said, "Next time I'm bringing two boxes, one for each."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
story:
The water at Camp Windrow had been pulling back all week, and by Tuesday the swim dock stood a full meter above the recession line, so the whole afternoon group had been herded to the archery range instead. Jaxon was fitting his third arrow when he heard the laughter start near the equipment shed. Henri was standing there holding a bow with a grip bent almost sideways, and a kid from another cabin was saying, "They gave the broken one to the kid who talks to arrows." A ring of maybe ten campers stood around, and every single one of them watched and nobody moved.

Jaxon nocked his arrow and pretended to aim while his brain churned. Last summer he had read a thing in his sister's psychology book, something about crowds. He couldn't remember the name of it at first, only the shape of it: the more people watching, the less likely any one of them was to do anything, because everybody figured somebody else would go first. He had thought it was nonsense then. Standing here now with his string half drawn, he wasn't so sure. He looked at Aydan, two targets over, who was clearly listening and clearly not moving. Aydan glanced at Jaxon, then at the ground.

The name surfaced at last, arriving the way forgotten homework does, all at once and too late to matter. "It's the bystander effect," Jaxon said quietly, mostly to himself.

"What?" Aydan said.

"Nothing. I think," Jaxon said, and lowered the bow. "If I go stand next to Henri, watch what happens." He set the arrow in the rack and walked over, slow, like he had a reason, and stopped at Henri's shoulder. "Hey," he said. "Trade you bows. This one's got a weird flex to it, I want to see something."

Henri blinked at him. "It's broken."

"I know. I'm testing an idea." Jaxon took the bent bow and turned it over with a small frown, as if it were genuinely interesting. The kid who had made the joke looked around, seemed to realize nobody was laughing anymore, and drifted back toward his own target.

Then Aydan came over, and after Aydan a girl from the third cabin, and then two more campers, until there were five people around Henri asking to see his stance, and the moment had folded itself up like a map and blown away. Jaxon kept his voice light and his eyes on the warped grip. One person moves, he thought, and the spell breaks. Or maybe the joke would have died anyway, and it was all ambiguous, cause and effect tangled up like fishing line. He filed that under things he couldn't prove.

Mr. Leblanc came by at the end of the hour to collect the equipment. He picked up the bent bow, turned it exactly the way Jaxon had, and said, "Who found this?"

"Henri did," Jaxon said. "It wasn't his fault it snapped."

Mr. Leblanc looked from Jaxon to Henri, then at the small crowd still hanging around Henri's target, helping him count his arrows back into the quiver. "Funny," Mr. Leblanc said slowly. "Usually nobody reports broken gear. It just turns up in the pile." He rested the bow against the shed and pulled out a clipboard. "Henri, you want to help me log it? You're the one who thrived out here today, three bullseyes on a crooked target."

Henri smiled for the first time all afternoon. "Bring the broken one," he told Jaxon, already walking. "I want to see your weird flex."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
The guidance counsellor's office smelled like pencil shavings and old paper. Natalie sat across from Mr. Chen's desk, twisting the strap of her backpack, while he rummaged through a drawer. On the desk between them sat a little tin airplane with a propeller that spun whenever the heater kicked on, and a poster on the wall showed faces with labels underneath: worried, calm, stressed. Mr. Chen was helping her with her schedule, but he kept getting interrupted, because Larissa had come in too, and Larissa could not stop talking about the swim tryouts on Thursday.

"I can't eat," Larissa said. She picked up the tin airplane and set it down again without spinning the propeller. "I keep thinking about the diving block. What if I false start? What if I freeze and everyone stares?" She had been saying things like this since Monday, and it was only Wednesday. Natalie watched her friend's hands open and close around the airplane and thought about her dog at home, who barked like the world was ending whenever the mail slot clattered. The dog forgot the mail slot the second it went quiet. Larissa's problem was different, and Natalie wanted to know why, because if she could name it, maybe she could fix it.

"The diving block isn't even in front of you right now," Natalie said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "There's no water in this room. But you're acting scared." She looked at the poster, at the face labelled anxious. Then a memory surfaced, something her aunt had said once: psychologists separate fear, which is a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, which is worry about a threat that might happen later. The dog had fear. Larissa had anxiety about something days away. Natalie decided to test it.

"Okay, hear me out," she said. "When that dog lunged at you at the park last spring, you were scared, but it was over in ten seconds and you were fine by dinner." Larissa nodded. "The tryout is Thursday. It hasn't happened. So this isn't the same kind of scared. Your brain is fighting a race that hasn't started." Larissa stared at her, then laughed, a small surprised sound. "That's weirdly better," she said. "Can we do something about it, though? My mom keeps telling me to calm down, and that signifies nothing."

Mr. Chen, who had been listening while pretending to sort files, raised one hand. "Boundaries, first," he said mildly. "I need to be explicit: this is my lunch break, so you two get ten minutes and the leftover pretzels." He slid the bag across the desk. Natalie grabbed a pretzel and pointed it at Larissa like a pen. "New rule. Every time you imagine the dive, you picture the tin airplane instead and say one true thing that's happening now. Warm office. Pretzel. Friend." Larissa picked up the airplane, spun the propeller with her thumb, and watched it blur. "Ten minutes," she said. "Teach me the airplane rule before the bell."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: In a first-past-the-post election, the candidate with the most votes in a district wins the seat, even if they did not get more than half the votes.
story:
Liam had never been inside city hall before Saturday, and the echo of his sneakers on the marble floor made him feel like he was going to get in trouble for something. Mr. Lin met them at the bottom of the staircase, holding a stack of ballots and a shoebox with a slot cut in the top. "Youth council mock election," he said. "Every vote gets counted today, right here in the council chamber. You three are my counting team."

Harley dumped out the ballots on the long wooden table where the real councillors sat on real meeting nights. There were forty of them, and Liam sorted them into piles by candidate while Reagan kept tally on a clipboard. The room smelled like dust and lemon polish. When the last ballot was sorted, the piles read twelve votes for the skateboard park, eleven for the community garden, and seventeen for the esports lounge. Reagan circled the seventeen. "Esports wins. That's it, then."

"Wait," Harley said, jabbing a finger at the piles. "Seventeen out of forty is less than half. Twenty-one would be half. So most people picked something else, and the esports lounge still gets everything?" Reagan was skeptical, recounting twice, but the numbers refused to change. Liam, who had privately despised the esports campaign from the start, was surprised to feel his stomach go wrong anyway. It wasn't only about losing. Twenty-three ballots had gone the other way, and they were all about to be swept into the shoebox like they'd never existed.

He lined the piles up like bars of a graph, which is what he did with everything, even the times he found organisms under his microscope at school. "What if we split it up instead," he said slowly. "Forty votes, and the esports lounge got close to half, and the garden and the park got close to a quarter each. There are four spots on the youth council budget. So the lounge takes two spots, and the garden and the park each take one." Reagan frowned. "That's not how elections work, though." Liam turned to Mr. Lin, who had been listening from the doorway with his arms folded, and asked whether both ways had names. "Yours is proportional representation," Mr. Lin said. "Reagan's is first past the post."

Mr. Lin wouldn't tell them which was fairer, because of course he wouldn't. So Liam proposed a deal he didn't love: keep first past the post for naming the youth council president, since Reagan pointed out somebody had to actually be in charge, but split the budget money proportionally, by the piles. Harley agreed for the garden side, Reagan agreed because the esports lounge still came out on top, and they wrote it all on the clipboard and carried it to Mr. Lin like a treaty.

The council chamber emptied out through the big doors and the lights clicked off in sections, each one a little clap of dark. Outside on the steps, Harley bumped his shoulder against Liam's. "Good fix." Liam looked back at the building, where somewhere inside his losing ballots were still sitting in the shoebox, unrecorded in any official tally, and where he'd also just handed the thing he despised the biggest share of the money. "Half a fix," he said. "Come on, I'll race you to the bus stop."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
story:
Brooklyn sat on the floor of Guillaume's basement with a camera lens in her lap, waiting while he hunted for batteries. The lens was his dad's, heavy as a soup can, and she kept her eyes on it so she would not think about the lines on her hips. She had seen them that morning in the mirror, thin and pale, like scratches that did not hurt. She had pulled her shirt down fast, before her brain could start guessing.

"Found them," Guillaume said, holding up two batteries. "Drew's coming with popcorn. His mom is frugal, so it's the store brand, but it's fine."

They were making a stop-motion movie about a LEGO knight who fought a vacuum cleaner. Brooklyn fit the lens onto the old camera and squinted through it. Everything looked closer and stranger, the knight's painted face full of tiny cracks. She liked that. Behind a lens, small things became important and big things became small.

Drew arrived with the popcorn and news. "Guess what. My sister had a total meltdown yesterday over her legs. She found these little lines on them and thought something was wrong with her skin."

Brooklyn's hands stopped on the camera. "What kind of lines?"

"Thin ones. Like little white threads. My mom said relax, it happens when you grow too fast for your skin to keep up." Drew shrugged and ate a handful of popcorn. "She says hers faded after a while."

Guillaume clicked the vacuum cleaner on for the knight's battle scene and its motor made everything rattle. Brooklyn did not laugh at it this time. She was thinking. She had grown two inches since September; Ms. Huang had said so at school when they got measured in gym, and Brooklyn's leggings had gone from long to short without her noticing the day it happened. Fast growing, then lines. She tested the idea quietly, matching it against what she knew. Drew's sister had shot up recently too; everyone said so.

After the movie was done, the knight victorious on a hill of popcorn kernels, Guillaume walked her to the door. "Same time next week?" he asked.

At home, Brooklyn found her mom folding laundry. "Mom, are the lines on people's skin, the thin ones, do they have a name?"

"Stretch marks," her mom said. "Lots of people get them during growth spurts, and they usually fade over time."

"Okay," Brooklyn said. That night she looked once more, quick, then pulled her shirt down and did not check again until Sunday. The lines were still there. She nodded at them the way you nod at a neighbor, and went to find her sketchbook to draw the knight.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Either person on a date can say no to holding hands, a hug or a kiss at any time, and a respectful partner accepts that answer without pressure.
story:
Arthur had rehearsed the plan three times on the bus: buy two hot chocolates, find Philip near the fence behind the away bleachers, and watch the fourth quarter together. It was the first date either of them had been on, and Arthur wanted it to go smoothly, which was exactly why he kept checking the plan like homework. He asked Philip earlier that day to clarify one detail, whether they were meeting at the fence or at the ticket booth, and Philip had said the fence, laughing a little, because of course the fence.

The game was close. The home team, whose mascot was a gray kangaroo suit with a sagging pouch, kept fumbling, and every time the marsupial slumped against the goalpost the crowd groaned along with it. Arthur and Philip stood shoulder to shoulder in the cold, steam rising off the paper cups, and when the home team recovered a fumble on the thirty-yard line Philip grabbed Arthur's sleeve without seeming to notice he'd done it. Arthur noticed. He noticed the whole drive, through the cold smell of mustard and wet metal bleachers, all the way to the field goal that sailed through the uprights and won the game.

Then Philip let go of the sleeve and said, "You can hold my hand, if you want. That's allowed." Arthur reached over. Halfway there he stopped, because something occurred to him. "Can either of us change our mind? Like, say no halfway through, or at the end, whenever?"

Philip nodded. "Either of us. Any time. And the other one just accepts it, no pressure, no asking why."

Arthur closed the last few inches and took his hand. It was warm from the cup and a little sticky from the cocoa. They walked out with the crowd, past the ticket booth where the cashier was counting quarters, past the mascot sitting on a cooler with the kangaroo head in its lap.

At the corner where they usually split up, Arthur turned toward Philip for a hug. Philip stepped back, just slightly, just enough. "Not tonight," he said. "Hand was good. Hug, no."

For one second Arthur felt the pull to make it a joke, to say something that would nudge Philip into changing his answer. He let the second pass. "Okay," he said. "See you Monday."

He walked home with his hands in his pockets, and his phone buzzed twice before he reached his block. The first text said, thanks for not making it weird. The second said, the kangaroo wants a rematch next Friday. Same fence?

Arthur typed one word back, "Fence," and hit send.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
story:
The dryer at home had gone completely silent that morning, and Romy decided it was extinct, like the dinosaurs, except with more lint. She dragged her bulging laundry bag to the bus stop and plopped it down on the bench just as Keaton skidded up beside her, breathless.

"Is that your entire wardrobe?" he asked, poking the bag. "What did you do, lose a bet?"

"Mom's home at six, and she said if the laundry isn't done by then, I'm the defendant in a trial I will lose. The dryer makes a buzz and then nothing. It's dead."

Keaton leaned on the bus stop sign. "Or it's faking. My grandma's toaster used to do that."

The bus wasn't due for eleven minutes, and the schedule seemed to fluctuate depending on the driver's mood, so Romy had time to think. She'd passed the laundromat a hundred times, and taped to its window was a poster she'd never actually read. She read it now, mentally: failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect. Lint. Airflow. Heat. She thought about the filter at home, which she had never once touched in her entire life, and a cold, prickly feeling crept up her neck. Nobody in her house had ever pulled that thing out. Ever.

"Change of plan," she said, hoisting the bag back up. "We're walking home. Two blocks. You're my witness."

"You just said the dryer is dead."

"I said extinct. Extinct animals sometimes turn out to be frogs in a hole. Come on."

At home she yanked open the dryer door, slid out the lint filter, and stared. A mat of grey fuzz sat on it, thick as a slice of bread, dense enough to bounce a coin off. Keaton made a noise like a startled goose. Romy peeled the whole felted slab away in one piece, held it up like evidence, and dropped it in the trash. Then she restarted the dryer. It buzzed, hesitated, and began to tumble with a low, healthy rumble.

"Your defendant," Keaton announced, "is found not guilty."

"Not guilty of being extinct," Romy agreed, feeding towels into the washing machine and starting the whole load from scratch, sorting darks from lights like she'd actually been paying attention all along. She folded the first warm shirt into a lopsided square and held it up. "Mom will never know. This stays between us, the dryer, and the lint."

"Your secret's safe," Keaton said, patting the machine gently on its corner. "So long as you feed it, it won't burn the house down."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Lifting the lid while rice simmers lets steam escape, which can leave the grains undercooked.
story:
The community kitchen smelled like toasted cumin and hot oil, and Camille stood at the counter with three timers in front of her and no idea how to use any of them. Her curry bubbled on the back burner, the flatbread dough rested under a damp cloth, and the pot of rice sat on the front burner with its lid rattling. The whole point of tonight's lesson, Mr. Islam had said, was that everything should arrive at the window together, hot, at the same moment. If the rice finished early it would go cold. If it finished late, the curry would thicken into paste.

Last week had been a disaster, and Camille remembered it in a quick, stomach-dropping flash: Patience standing over the rice pot, lifting the lid every two minutes to check on it, saying "just looking," while Kamden shouted that the flatbread was burning. Every dish had finished at a different time. The rice had come out crunchy in the middle, and they had eaten standing up, in shifts, and Camille had gone home with the sour feeling that she had missed something she should have seen.

She thought about that crunchy rice all week. The pot had been on the heat for the right amount of time. The water had been measured. So why had the grains stayed hard? She turned it over while walking to school, while washing dishes at home. The difference was Patience's lifting, again and again. Something was escaping each time that lid came off. Steam. The steam was part of the cooking, and Patience had been letting it out.

"Patience," she said now, "don't open that pot. Trust me on this one." Patience's hand was already halfway to the handle.

"But I can't tell if it's working," Patience said. "It's an illusion, just sitting there doing nothing."

"That's what it looks like, but it's not nothing. Last week you kept checking and the rice came out crunchy." Camille slid a strip of tape across the lid and the pot rim, sealing it like a tiny door. "We leave it alone."

Patience looked wounded, so Kamden leaned over to reassure her. "You can be in charge of the flatbread instead. That one actually needs watching." He flipped a puffed golden round onto the plate and she grabbed the spatula, and soon she was too busy turning bread to glance at the taped pot at all.

Camille timed the curry down to its last ten minutes, dropped the flatbread rounds onto the griddle so they'd be warm and soft when the rice was done, and then, when everything was close, she pulled the tape free and lifted the lid herself. Steam rolled up in one thick white cloud, fragrant and perfect, and the grains below were separate and tender all the way through. She spooned rice onto three plates, ladled curry beside it, and slid the warm bread on top just as Mr. Islam called time.

"All together," Patience said, staring at the three plates.

Camille picked up the first plate and carried it to the window.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Sophia stabbed her noodle and slid her phone across the table to Harper. "Look at this invite. My aunt's wedding is Saturday, and it says wear white if you can. My mom says I can't."

Harper leaned over, chopsticks frozen midair. "Weird. Since when does a wedding want everyone in white?"

"That's what I said. But look at the photo." Sophia enlarged it. The bride, Great-Aunt Mei, stood in a red dress with gold stitching, glowing like a lantern. "She's not wearing white. Everyone else is, in the picture from her first ceremony announcement."

Louis reached across and scrolled. "So the guests wear white and the bride wears red? That's backwards."

"Maybe it's a theme," Harper said. "Like a white party."

Sophia's mother set down a bowl of soup and shook her head. "Not a theme. Your great-aunt is honoring tradition. In our family's culture, white is worn for mourning at funerals." She spooned dumplings into Louis's bowl without pausing. "So the bride does not wear it. But your cousin Clara's fiancé's family is American, and for them the bride wears white at weddings. Same color, opposite meanings."

"Wait," Louis said. "The same color can mean two opposite things?"

"Apparently," Sophia's mother said, and went back to the kitchen.

The three of them sat quietly for a moment. Sophia turned her fork over, thinking. Everyone at that wedding would be looking at the same white dress and seeing something completely different, depending on where they came from. Her mom hadn't explained why the traditions existed, and Sophia didn't ask, because the important part was already clear: meaning wasn't in the color itself. It was in the people looking at it.

"So what do I actually wear?" Sophia pulled up photos of her closet on her phone. "I have until Friday to decide. If I wear white, Clara's side thinks I'm festive. If Aunt Mei's side sees it that way too, because they chose this, fine. But what if some older relatives didn't get the memo?"

Harper grinned. "Test it. Text your mom's cousin and ask what everyone wore at the engagement party."

Sophia did. The reply came back fast: a photo of a room full of guests in white and ivory, laughing, with Aunt Mei in red at the center. Sophia counted the faces, then tried to quantify her worry on a scale of one to ten and decided it had dropped to about a two. "It worked for them," she said. "The families already negotiated this."

"Negotiated a color," Louis said. "That's like commerce for clothes."

Saturday morning, Sophia buttoned the white dress she'd borrowed from Harper and felt cautiously optimistic. At the reception, Clara's grandmother complimented her outfit, and Aunt Mei's brother gave her a thumbs-up from across the room. Two sides of one family, one table, one color doing double duty.

Sophia found Aunt Mei near the cake. "I almost didn't wear this."

Aunt Mei smoothed Sophia's sleeve and smiled. "White for the guests, red for me. Everyone sees what they hoped to see."

"Which did you see?" Sophia asked.

Aunt Mei lifted her champagne glass. "I saw a girl who asked a good question before she got dressed."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
