fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
story:
Sebastian jogged the chain-link loop that circled the community pool, counting strides while Caroline timed him from a folding chair by the gate. Eight hundred metres was two laps of the loop, and every time he raced Greyson after school, he died on the second one. "Two twenty-one for the first lap," Caroline called, "and then you basically walked." She was studying for her lifeguard written test between splits, flashcards about chlorine levels spread across her knees, because she wanted the summer job more than anything and needed to pass by Friday.

"You're starting too slow," Greyson insisted from the deep end, where he was treading water between sets. "You save too much. Then you sprint at the end like it's a hundred."

Sebastian didn't think so. He had watched the men's eight-hundred-metre world record race from the 2012 London Olympics on his phone three times the night before, David Rudisha running alone at the front, and something about it had snagged in his head. He asked Caroline to watch it with him now, the phone propped on her chair, the pool's gutter dripping behind the audio. On the second viewing she paused the screen and tapped the split that flashed after the first lap. "Look at this. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second." Greyson hauled himself out to see, dripping on the concrete. "The world record, and he slows down at the end?" He sounded almost offended.

Sebastian ran it again in his head. The champion went out fast, faster than his finishing pace, and still won the world. Maybe the problem wasn't that Sebastian started too fast. Maybe he started too slow, spent the whole first lap trapped behind his own caution, and then had nothing left because he panicked and surged at the wrong moments. There was no way to see pacing, no way to hold it in your hand, but you could test it. "One more time," he told Caroline. "First lap, I'm going out like it's a four hundred. Don't yell at me."

He went through the first lap so hard the roar of his own pulse drowned the pool filter, past the barren shade of the empty baby pool, through the chlorine smell at the gate, his legs already heavy when Caroline shouted the split. Two fifteen. His best opening ever. The second lap hurt more than anything he could remember, and he gripped the fence and gasped, certain he had ruined it. "Two twenty-two," Caroline called, and then, checking her watch twice, "Three thirty-seven total. You just took eleven seconds off."

Greyson stood there with his towel forgotten over one shoulder. "Do it again Tuesday?" Sebastian was already walking the curve to cool down, one hand pressed to his aching side, grinning so wide it hurt worse than his legs. "Bring the flashcards," he told Caroline. "I'll time you on the written stuff while I recover."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: During a severe drought on Daphne Major in 1977, small seeds ran out, and medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because they could crack large, hard seeds.
story:
Ellie's science grade was currently a C minus, which her mother described as "room to grow" and which Ellie described, privately and more accurately, as a problem. Mr. Marino had assigned the final project: explain how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands. Kai was building a pioneer settlement for social studies and kept offering her leftover fence posts. Benoit said he was doing his on volcanoes, which was not even the right unit.

Ellie started with a shoebox and some clay birds, but the birds all looked like pigeons with identity issues. Worse, she could not actually say what she was supposed to say. The textbook had a picture of a small scrubby island called Daphne Major and a paragraph she had read four times. During a severe drought in 1977, the small seeds ran out, and medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because they could crack the large, hard seeds that were left. She could recite it. She could not explain it to a six-year-old, and Mr. Marino had announced that anyone who could not explain it to a six-year-old did not understand it themselves.

"Then be the six-year-old," she told Kai on Thursday, dragging him to the cafeteria table where she had dumped a bag of birdseed and two pairs of pliers.

"I'm twelve."

"Pretend." She sorted the seed into two piles, small soft ones and large hard ones, then took the small pile away. "Drought. Small seeds are gone. Pick a bird." She handed him the pliers with the narrow tips and kept the wide-jawed ones for herself. Benoit sat down uninvited, which was how Benoit sat down anywhere.

They cracked seeds. Kai's narrow tips slipped off the big hard ones, and after a minute he was grinding the same seed against the table with an expression of personal betrayal. Ellie's wide jaws split them, one after another, though she had to regulate her grip carefully because squeezing too hard just launched the seed kernel across the cafeteria. A kernel hit Benoit in the ear. He ate it.

"So the big-beaked ones ate, and the other ones didn't," Kai said, spitting out a crushed seed. "And then?"

"And then the survivors had babies, and the babies had the useful beaks, and the island full of birds slowly had different beak shapes than the finches on the other islands." She lined up her clay lumps, which still looked like pigeons, and squeezed the front of each one forward into a stubby deep wedge. They now looked like pigeons with unfortunate noses, but the noses were the point.

On presentation day, Mr. Marino watched her pliers demonstration without expression, arms folded, the way a bench watches a chess match. Then he asked the class who survived the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, and Ellie answered before anyone else could, "Medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks, because they could crack the large, hard seeds after the small ones ran out." Mr. Marino wrote something in his book.

"A minus," he said, and turned to Benoit's volcano, which was already leaking baking soda onto the floor.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: When a variable appears on both sides, as in 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, subtracting 3x from both sides gathers the variable on one side: 2x + 2 = 10.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled like pencil shavings and old carpet, and Alexia had been staring at the same problem for ten minutes. On her worksheet, in her own handwriting, it said 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, and she had no idea which x she was supposed to deal with first.

"If I get this wrong again, Ms. Johansson will think I wasn't listening," she whispered to Mehtab, who sat beside her with a science textbook open, drawing labelled arrows toward a picture of a microbe.

"Then don't get it wrong," Mehtab said, without looking up. "But you won't learn anything if I just hand you the answer."

Alexia slid her paper toward him anyway. "Look. There's an x on the left and an x on the right. Which one moves?"

Mehtab finally closed the textbook. "Try one. Pick either."

"That's ridiculous. One of them has to be the right one."

"Try the right side first. Take away the 3x."

Alexia wrote it out, crossing off the 3x with a careful line. Then, because Ms. Johansson had drilled it into the whole room that whatever you did to one side you did to the other, she subtracted 3x from the left too. She looked at what remained and sat back. Both x's had gathered onto one side, and the whole thing had shrunk to 2x + 2 = 10.

"That's it?" she said. "That's the whole trick?"

"Now do the other way," Mehtab said. "Take away the 5x instead."

She started a fresh line. When she subtracted 5x from both sides this time, she got negative numbers, but the x's still ended up alone on a single side. It was messier, and she wrinkled her nose at the minus signs, but it worked too. Either x. Both ways. She checked by finishing the first version: 2x + 2 = 10 meant 2x = 8, so x = 4. She plugged 4 back into the original problem, and both sides came out to 22.

Ms. Johansson drifted over and scanned the page. "Two methods, both correct, and a check. Nicely done, Alexia."

Faith leaned across from the next table, where she had been muttering that fractions were toxic. "Wait, it works both directions? Show me that on mine."

Alexia pulled Faith's paper over and uncapped her pen. "Okay, yours is 6x + 3 = 4x + 11. Watch what happens when I take away 4x."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
Ariana had been watching the same page for a week: Avah's handmade bracelets, woven from silver thread and blue beads, listed at eighteen dollars each in the school's online marketplace. On Friday night, Ariana checked one last time before bed, feeling almost nocturnal the way she kept waking to refresh the page, and every single bracelet was gone. Sold out. At eighteen dollars.

"I want to hypothesize something," she told Noa at lunch on Monday. "If Avah can sell thread and beads for eighteen dollars, could we?" Noa shrugged and said her cousin had a law of supply poster in her shop. So Ariana and Noa spent their savings, plus the ten dollars Ariana's grandmother sent from her pension every month, on supplies. They listed ten bracelets at sixteen dollars.

They sold out in two days. Ariana raised the price to eighteen, then twenty, and the bracelets still went fast. It felt like discovering an invisible rule, something she couldn't see directly but could test. "Watch," she told Noa. "The price is high, so I predict more people will start selling."

By the next week, her prediction had come true in a way she hadn't expected. Ms. Kerr, who lived two streets over, posted a page of beaded bracelets. Then two girls from the chess club. Then a boy Ariana had never met, selling woven bracelets at fifteen dollars, then twelve. The marketplace page that had shown only Avah's work now scrolled on and on. Ariana checked her own listing. Two bracelets sat unsold for three days straight.

"So that's it," Noa said, scrolling beside her. "When the price went up, everybody started offering more. That's the law of supply." Ariana nodded slowly. The rule she had guessed at was real, and it had a name, and it was now working against her. She couldn't change how many sellers there were. But she could change what she made.

That weekend Ariana and Noa didn't weave bracelets. Instead they braided keychains with tiny lightning bolts worked into the pattern, something nobody else on the page was selling. They listed five at ten dollars each. By Monday morning, three had sold, and a message waited in her inbox from the boy with the fifteen-dollar bracelets.

"Hey," it read. "Where did you get those bolt beads?"

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A person's reaction time on a stopwatch is often about a fifth of a second, so timing a longer run makes that error matter less.
story:
Emmett crouched at the mouth of his garage, holding a marble against the sloped ramp he had built from an old shelf board and two paint cans. Ayaan stood beside him with a stopwatch, and Aksel crouched farther down the driveway with a second stopwatch and a strip of masking tape stuck to the concrete.

"Same roll, two timers," Emmett said. "One of these numbers has to be lying."

Ayaan's dad had offered the garage for the project because it had the only smooth, level floor on the street, and because rain was coming. Emmett needed a distance-time graph for Monday, which meant he needed real distances and real times, not numbers he invented at his desk. A graph built from made-up points would be counterfeit science, and Mr. Torres had a nose for that sort of thing.

He let the marble go. It hissed down the ramp, crossed the tape, and rattled into a rolled-up towel Aksel had placed at the end.

"Two point one two seconds," Ayaan read off.

Aksel squinted at his own screen. "One point nine five."

They ran it again. Two point zero nine and one point eight eight. A third roll gave two point three one against two point one four. Every time, Aksel's number came out smaller, and the gap between them stayed about the same, close to a fifth of a second, whether the marble ran fast or slow.

"It's not the marble," Emmett said slowly. "The marble doesn't care who's watching it."

Ayaan frowned. "So it's us."

Emmett made them both close their eyes and try to snap their fingers the instant he clapped. Aksel snapped almost with the clap. Ayaan snapped late, every single time. It was small, that delay, but it was there, like a hiccup in the middle of the count.

Ayaan's face went pink. "I'm messing up your whole project."

"You're messing it up the same amount every time," Emmett said, and then he stopped, because the idea arrived all at once. "Wait. That's the thing."

He grabbed the chalk they had been using to mark distances and drew a new start line way back near the garage door, tripling the run. "We take a census," he said, waving at the tape marks, "of lots of rolls, the long ones, and your late click gets spread out. It's a fifth of a second, so on a short run it eats a huge bite of the answer. On a long run it barely matters."

They rolled the marble ten times down the full length. Ayaan's times and Aksel's times came out nearly twins, two tenths apart at most, and often closer. Emmett wrote each pair in his notebook, averaged them, and plotted the points on graph paper taped to the garage wall. The dots climbed into a nearly straight line.

"That's the speed," he said, tapping the slope with his pencil. "Right there."

Ayaan leaned in and ran a finger along the line. "So my slow thumb didn't ruin anything."

"It's part of the data now," Emmett said. "Every scientist has a thumb."

Aksel set up the ramp again without being asked, and outside the first fat drops began to slap the driveway.

"One more roll," Emmett said, pressing the marble to the board. "On three."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
story:
Aiden stood in his grandfather's study with a photocopied page of Hebrew in his hand and a month until his bar mitzvah, and the letters refused to stay in order. His grandfather had read from the Torah scroll at his own bar mitzvah, decades ago in a synagogue that no longer existed, and he had promised Aiden one thing: he would teach him the way he had been taught, with the scroll itself.

"Tomorrow you'll practice on the real thing," his grandfather said, laying a velvet cover over the scroll on the desk. "Tonight, again from the page."

Aiden read the blessing aloud twice, stumbled on the same phrase twice, and wondered whether his tongue was simply obstinate or whether the words moved around when he blinked. He tried closing his eyes between lines to see if the pattern would settle. It didn't. He tried tapping the rhythm on the desk with two fingers, and that helped a little, the way a drumbeat holds a marching line together.

The next evening his grandfather unrolled the scroll across the long table, and Aiden leaned over the parchment. The letters were square and black, the columns neat as a field after planting. He began to read, following his place with his eyes, but as the tricky phrase came near, his finger drifted up and hovered an inch above the page, tracing the words as if his hand could steady them. His grandfather reached into the desk drawer without a word and held out a slim silver rod with a hand-shaped point at the tip.

"Use the yad," he said. "It means hand."

Aiden took it. The metal was cool and heavier than it looked. He set the pointing finger under the first word of the phrase and read on, and this time the letters held still, as though something about touching the place without touching had anchored them. Was it the yad, or was it that he now had to monitor two things at once, the words and the pointer, so his mind couldn't wander off and drag the syllables with it? He decided to test it. He read the next verse using the yad, then one without it, then one with it again. Without it, his finger crept toward the parchment; with it, his place stayed locked.

"Why not just touch it with a finger?" he asked.

"The parchment isn't touched," his grandfather said, and rolled the corner of the scroll back a little. "Not by hands."

On Saturday, in front of everyone, his mother in the second row and his classmates Tanner and Carys squeezed beside her, Aiden stood at the reading table. The rabbi handed him the yad, its silver hand catching the light from the windows. He set it beneath the first word and read, all the way through, without a single stumble, and when he finished, the whole room rose around him, and his grandfather's voice was the loudest one there.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
story:
Antoine had been practising his wheelie for twenty minutes when Troy started in on Katie's dinosaur backpack.

"Nice bag," Troy said, loud enough for the kids on the swings to hear. "Did you dig it up yourself?"

A few kids laughed. Katie stood by the climbing wall, holding one strap like she was thinking about bolting for the gate.

Antoine's first idea was to say something clever back, but he'd tried that last week and it had turned into a ten-minute insult contest that Troy won. So he sat on his bike and thought instead. Troy wasn't even looking at Katie when he joked. He was looking at the kids on the swings. That was the interesting part. It was like the teasing needed people watching it, the way a fire needs air. Take away the audience and the whole thing might just go out.

He ran a quick test in his head. If he yelled at Troy, everyone would gather closer, and Troy would have to keep going to save face. If he did nothing, Katie stood there alone. There was a third door, though.

Antoine dropped his bike in the grass and walked over to Katie like he hadn't heard any of it. "Come on, let's go," he said. "I need help with the water fountain. It's got an intricate system of buttons and I can't figure out which one actually works."

Katie blinked, then caught on. "The one on the left," she said, following him. "Everyone knows the left one."

"Left, right, up, down," Antoine said as they walked off. "It's like a whole curriculum in fountain studies. There should be a test."

The swings had gone quiet behind them. By the time they reached the fountain, Troy's joke had nobody left to land on, and it just sort of evaporated, the way a balloon goes floppy when you let go of the neck.

At the fountain, Katie pressed the left button and it sprayed Antoine's shoe. "Oops," she said, grinning for the first time all recess.

Tuesday morning, Antoine found a folded note tucked into his backpack pocket. In Katie's handwriting it said: "Thanks for yesterday. Troy cornered me by the buses but nobody was around, and he gave up after like ten seconds. Weird. Anyway, dinosaur backpack forever. K." Antoine read it twice, then added it to the small collection of important papers in his desk at home, next to a library card and a drawing of a shark wearing a hat.

At recess, Troy came over to the basketball court, bouncing a ball with more force than the situation required. "Okay," he said. "The fountain thing. That was actually pretty smooth, and now everyone thinks I'm the boring kid who can't keep a joke going."

"You could sustain a joke for weeks," Antoine said. "That's not your problem."

Troy spun the ball on one finger, watched it wobble, and caught it. "Fine. But if I'm going to be funny, I'm going to be funny at someone who deserves it. Like Mr. Pell, who assigns homework on Fridays."

"That's a bold target," Antoine said.

Katie appeared beside them with her dinosaur backpack swinging. "For Mr. Pell, you're going to need a better plan than a backpack joke," she said, and passed Troy the ball.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Rising action is the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax.
story:
Mr. Leblanc handed the stories back on Tuesday, and Landon's had one comment in red at the bottom: "Your dragon attack is great, but I got there too fast. Fix the middle." Landon read it three times during lunch, scowling at the page while Hope peeled an orange beside him.

"My story's fine," he said. "The knight fights the dragon on page one. That's the best part."

Hope shrugged. "Then why did he write fix the middle?"

That afternoon Landon asked Malachi to read it, mostly to prove Mr. Leblanc wrong. Malachi read fast, the way he did everything, then flipped back to the first page. "It's all fight," he said. "The knight wins, story over. There's nothing to be scared of. It's like when we watched that movie trailer that showed the whole movie."

Landon took the pages back. That night he tried an experiment. He took his sister's favorite book, the one with the prism on the cover that split light into rainbows on her wall, and copied its shape. Not the words, just the pattern: small trouble, bigger trouble, worst trouble, then the huge moment. He wrote the pattern out on a sticky note like a diagram. Page one, the knight's village loses its water. Page two, a stranger takes the last horse. Page three, the knight's brother is taken. Then the dragon.

The next morning he left a note in Hope's locker because he got to school before she did. "Read this version. Don't look at page one first. Tell me if your stomach hurts before the end." After first period she found him by the water fountain, holding the pages like evidence. "Page two," she said. "When the brother gets taken, I actually gripped the paper. That didn't happen yesterday."

"So it works," Landon said.

"What do you call that part? The stacking-up part?"

Landon had looked it up the night before, in the writing handbook Mr. Leblanc kept on the shelf by the window. "Rising action," he said. "It's the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax." He said it fast, the way you recite something you just learned, and Hope nodded like it was obvious.

In class, Mr. Leblanc read the new draft silently, his face neutral, and Landon could not tell anything from it. Then Mr. Leblanc slid the paper across the desk. "Better. Could you replicate this structure in your next one, without copying the plot?" Landon said he could, and he meant it, because now he understood it wasn't about the dragon at all.

At lunch Malachi grabbed the pages out of his binder before Landon could stop him. "You added a brother?" Malaci read, and read, and for once in his life he did not rush. When he finished the last page he looked up and said, "Read me the water part again. I want to hear how you did that."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks.
story:
Julia stood at the folding table in the community room of Maple Court, the seniors' residence, trying to remember which crate held the canned peas. A hand-lettered sign above her read Community Food Bank, and beside it a poster with a stylized bowl logo she'd never paid attention to before. She was hesitant at first about handing out the wrong thing, but the woman in the purple cardigan waiting in front of her just smiled and said she'd take whatever Julia had.

"If you like peas, these are good," Julia said, and the woman took two cans and moved on to Forrest, who was bagging bread at the next table.

Outside, a white truck backed up to the loading door, and Julia squinted at it. The same bowl logo from the poster was printed on its door, and under it, in small letters, a city name from two states away. She nudged Forrest. "Why is that truck from Ohio? Isn't this our town's food bank?"

Forrest shrugged and went back to sorting oranges. Ty, who had been hauling boxes since seven, said maybe the truck was just lost. But Julia kept thinking about it while she restocked crackers. A second truck arrived at ten, from a different city entirely, and it had the same logo too. Lost trucks didn't travel in pairs with matching paint.

During the lull before lunch, she found Ms. Shapiro, the volunteer coordinator, checking clipboards near the kitchen. Ms. Shapiro governed the whole operation from a desk no bigger than a cookie sheet, deciding who worked which table and what got unloaded first. "Can I ask you something?" Julia said. "Both trucks today have that bowl logo, but they're from different places. Are they all the same food bank?"

"Same network," Ms. Shapiro said. "It's called Feeding America. More than 200 food banks, all across the United States, in one nationwide network."

Julia turned that over while she stacked juice boxes. One network, more than 200 food banks. That meant the crates of peanut butter weren't random; they had come through a system bigger than this one building. She decided to test it. The next time a driver came through the door, she asked to see his paperwork, and there it was again, the bowl logo at the top of a delivery slip from yet another city.

"See?" she said to Forrest, holding up the slip. "It's not our food bank and their food bank. They're all connected."

At the end of the afternoon, the woman in the purple cardigan came back for the last loaf of bread. Julia set it in her bag and added a jar of applesauce from the surplus crate. "I saved this for you," she said. "I noticed you took the small cans last time."

The woman patted her hand. "You watch out for people, don't you."

Julia taped the delivery slip, logo up, onto the edge of her folding table.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
story:
Jacob had never needed deodorant before this year, and that was the part that bugged him. He sat on Tony's front step with a bottle of water, shirt stuck to his back, after forty minutes of driveway basketball in the heat. Tony's older cousin, who was staying with them for the summer, dropped into the chair beside him with his own bottle.

"You reek," the cousin said to Tony.

"So do you," said Tony.

"I don't, actually." The cousin held out his arm and sniffed it. "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Body odor shows up when the bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from your armpit glands. Those glands don't even turn on until puberty."

Jacob looked down at his own soaked shirt. "So we're just old enough to be a lunch buffet for germs now."

"Pretty much," the cousin said, and went inside.

Jacob carried the thought home the way you carry a rock in your shoe. Two days later he had a plan. He took two clean washcloths, wiped one across his forehead right after running, and tucked it into a plastic bag. Then he wiped the second one under his arm and put it in a second bag. He labeled them with tape and a marker: forehead, armpit. He set both bags on top of the heating vent, because the thermostat in the hallway said the house was cold and the vent was the warmest spot he knew. Warmth had to matter. His gym clothes only smelled bad after they sat crumpled in his locker, never right after class.

At Tony's house that afternoon, he explained the experiment. Tony's mom let them use the kitchen timer. Ariella came over because Tony texted her, and she leaned on the counter examining the bags like they were evidence.

"So your theory," she said, "is that it's not the sweating. It's what happens after."

"If I'm right, the armpit cloth will smell and the forehead cloth won't, even though both got sweat on them at the same time," Jacob said. "The forehead kind of sweat was fine last year. The armpit kind is the new stuff."

Tony wrinkled his nose. "You're doing science on your own stink."

"Somebody has to."

They waited an hour, and when the timer beeped, Jacob opened the forehead bag first. He sniffed, then passed it around. Nothing. Ariella smelled it twice and shrugged. Then Jacob opened the armpit bag, and Tony recoiled so fast he knocked his chair over. The smell was sour and unmistakable, like the whole locker room in one square of cloth.

"So the bacteria eat it," Ariella said slowly, "and that's the smell. The sweat itself is innocent."

Jacob taped both cloths to a sheet of paper and wrote the date underneath. He had a whole row of questions now. He wondered whether washing actually removed the bacteria or just scattered them, and whether the same trick would work on his gym shoes, which had been a mystery to him since October. He also wondered about the second gym shirt in his locker, the one he'd crumpled up wet on Monday and forgotten about until Friday. He looked at the taped cloth, then at his backpack hanging on the chair.

"Nobody touch anything," he said. "I have to go check on something."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
The rumor arrived on a Tuesday, in the seventh-grade group chat someone had optimistically named Homework Help. "Everyone knows Liliana took the fundraiser money," Ayaan wrote, and then three other people said some version of the same thing. By Thursday the message had been reposted, screenshotted, and restated so many times that Harper couldn't scroll past it without seeing Liliana's name attached to the word "sketchy." Nobody posted a receipt. Nobody posted a photo of an empty cash box. They just kept saying it, and the saying itself seemed to be the proof.

Harper noticed something odd about herself, though. On Tuesday she had thought the rumor was ridiculous, because Liliana had once chased her half a block to return a dropped bus pass. By Thursday, some quiet part of her brain had started to feel that it was plausible. Not proven. Just... likely. And she couldn't point to a single new piece of evidence, because there wasn't one. What had changed was the number of times she'd read the sentence.

She decided to run a test. In the chat she posted, in a casual tone, "fun fact: the vending machine on the second floor is being removed because it sold expired yogurt." Then she logged in as nobody in particular and repeated it. She reworded it slightly the second time, because a good scientist modifies the conditions a little, and waited. By lunch, someone had replied, "yeah I heard that too," and someone else had written, "my cousin goes here and she said the yogurt thing is real." Harper had invented the yogurt thing eleven minutes earlier.

She looked up what was going on and found a stack of search results. "Listen to this," she typed to Ayaan in a private message. "In 1977, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues did a study and found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true." Ayaan replied with a single wide-eyed emoji, then: "so the chat has basically been running the experiment on us for free."

Harper went back into the main chat and posted her evidence, screenshots and all: the invented yogurt rumor, the timeline, the original posts about Liliana with no source behind them. She pointed out the loaded words, the "everyone knows," the way a kid had even claimed some streamer had mentioned it, as if a person with a million followers would know what happened in their cafeteria. The typing dots bubbled up and vanished several times. Then a message landed from Ms. Chowdhury, who had apparently been added to the chat at some point and reading silently, which was its own kind of horror: "Harper, see me after class. Bring the screenshots."

Ayaan sent her one last message before the bell. "Expired yogurt," he wrote. "Never change."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
Max had forty minutes until the rehearsal at Hartwell Concert Hall, and one page of music that might as well have been written in code. The title, "Morning Walk," was followed by a scattering of Italian words: largo, then andante, then allegro near the end. Mr. Watanabe had handed out the sheets that morning and said only, "Trust the words, not your habits." Max had shoved the pages into his durable black folder and forgotten about them until now.

He found Jaya and Rose in the third row of the hall, already assembling their music stands. The place smelled like dust and lemon polish, and the stage lights transmitted a warm amber glow across the empty seats. Max climbed up beside them and set his folder on the stand. "I think I've got it," he said. "Largo must be the big finish, right? It sounds like 'large.' And andante sounds quick, like 'ante up.' So we start fast and get bigger."

Rose frowned at her page. "The citation at the bottom says the arranger lived in Milan. Maybe the words are just, like, style names."

"Style names, speed names, same thing," Max said. "Let's just play it."

They counted in together, Max on piano, Jaya on flute, Rose on snare drum. Max launched into the opening at a gallop, loud and proud, and the whole thing collapsed within eight bars. Jaya's flute line wandered off, Rose's rim-taps scrambled to catch up, and the melody that was supposed to unfold gently became a stampede. Mr. Watanabe's voice floated down from the balcony. "Again. Slower. Read the page."

Max stared at the sheet, cheeks hot. The problem wasn't his fingers; they knew the notes. The problem was something invisible on the page, some rule hiding inside those words. He thought about the title again. Morning Walk. A walk. Andante. Walking pace. He flipped his pencil over and wrote the words in a column: largo, andante, allegro. If andante was walking speed, then largo, sitting before it, had to be even slower, and allegro, at the end, had to be the fast part. The piece was a story that sped up, not one that started fast.

"Andante means at a walking pace," he said slowly, testing it out loud. "That's why it fell apart. I was running through a walk." Jaya tapped the first measure. "So largo is very slow, like barely moving, and allegro is fast and lively at the end." Rose grinned and loosened her drum key a quarter turn. "Finally, a plan."

They played it again. The opening stretched out, long and quiet as fog over a field. When the andante section arrived, Max let his hands settle into the easy rhythm of footsteps, and Jaya's flute floated in on top of it. By the allegro, the hall itself seemed to wake up, Rose's drum snapping like popcorn, the last chord ringing out into the high dark ceiling. Mr. Watanabe came down the stairs applauding, and Jaya slid her flute case over so there was room for him to sit.

"Same time Thursday," he said. "And Max, bring the pencil. It's doing good work."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer.
story:
Aubrey sat at the kitchen table with her math notebook open to a page that said, in her own handwriting, PROBLEM SET FROM HELL. She was supposed to solve linear equations by doing the same thing to both sides, which had seemed easy in class and now seemed like a trick someone was playing on her specifically. Her dad had told her the practice would pay off in a cumulative way, all the skills stacking up. She had said "mm" and taken her notebook to the kitchen, where the snacks were.

She had just gotten x to equal 4 on her third try when Neil texted her a photo. It was a photo of the whiteboard from math club, which had preceded her dad's kitchen by forty minutes in her evening, and which she had skipped to eat leftover pizza. On the board, in Neil's handwriting, was a "proof" that 1 equals 2. Below it, Marlowe had written CHECKMATE, MATH.

Aubrey set down her pencil and copied the steps onto her own page. Start with a equals b. Multiply both sides by a. Subtract b squared from both sides. Factor. So far so legal; she checked each line by doing the operation to both sides, the way Ms. Clarke had drilled into them until it was basically muscle memory. Then the proof divided both sides by a minus b, and one line later declared that 1 equals 2, with a little flourish.

Aubrey stared at the step. She tried it with real numbers. If a equals b, say both of them are 5, then a minus b is 5 minus 5, which is 0. She wrote it out. The proof had divided both sides by zero. She remembered Marlowe, of all people, saying it at lunch last week, mouth full of sandwich: "You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer." Aubrey had assumed Marlowe was quoting a fortune cookie. Apparently it was load-bearing.

She texted back: division by zero, step 5. Also she's right, and I owe Marlowe a cookie. Then, because the kitchen table was right there and the pizza was gone, she went back to her problem set. The equations behaved now that she watched what she did to both sides, dividing only by actual numbers, never zero, like she was checking a label for something she was allergic to and had wisely skipped the antibiotic.

Neil texted back a single word: traitor. Aubrey picked up her pencil and solved for x.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Anthony had one job on a Saturday afternoon at the mall: find a birthday present for his mother before her dinner at seven. He had twenty dollars and an hour, and Axton had tagged along because he was bored.

In the electronics store, Gurleen from his homeroom was standing at a display laptop, typing fast. "Look at this," she said when she saw them. "Remember my old craft blog from fifth grade? I found it. Every single post."

"How?" Anthony asked. "You deleted it last year. You said so."

She turned the laptop toward him. The page looked old, the banner crooked, a photo of her bracelet instructions sitting there like it had never left. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages," she said. "This part of it is called the Wayback Machine. Anyone can look at old versions of websites. Axton, try yours."

Axton typed the address of a video channel he had abandoned in sixth grade. A saved copy came up, dated three years back, complete with a map widget on the sidebar showing his old neighborhood. "That was my location thing," he said quietly. "I forgot I turned that on."

Anthony pulled out his phone and typed in the blog address he had used in fifth grade, the one with his skateboard tricks. The page loaded. There was his face, twelve years old, grinning in front of his house with the street number visible on the door. Below it, a post that read "gone to Riverside Skate Park every Saturday, come find me." He had written that when he was naive enough to think only his friends read it. Strangers could have read it too, at the time, and they still could, because here it was, saved.

"It's like donating something without knowing," Gurleen said. "I put that stuff up, and some archive took a copy and stored it. I never agreed to that exactly, but it's public, so it happened anyway."

Anthony tested it. He went to the top of the page and clicked through the list of dates, and the site had been saved eight separate times, each one a snapshot, like the mall directory board that photographed the food court every hour. Nothing he did on his phone now could remove those copies. His Saturday location, posted by his twelve-year-old self, was still findable by anyone with his old web address.

He screenshotted the page for himself, then closed the phone and got back to the present problem. In the candle shop near the escalator he found a lavender candle for fourteen dollars, paid the cashier, and still had time left.

"At least we know now," Gurleen said, catching up with him by the fountain.

"Yeah," Anthony said. "Check your old accounts before you post anything new." He dropped the candle in his backpack and headed for the exit doors.
